position_a: Edit directly in the Audio File Editor for speed and certainty
position_b: Keep all edits region-based or on duplicated files
what_decides: Use destructive processing only when the source is archived, the change is approved, and file-wide behavior is intended.

position_a: Mute every gap for maximum cleanliness
position_b: Preserve continuous room tone between phrases
what_decides: The noise floor, exposure of the section, number of layers, and audibility of gating determine the better approach.

position_a: Use a gate or Remove Silence for all cleanup
position_b: Edit gaps manually with fades and region gain
what_decides: Consistency and volume of the noise favor automation; exposed phrases and irregular material favor manual control.

position_a: Remove breaths for a polished vocal
position_b: Reduce only distracting breaths and preserve phrasing
what_decides: Genre, intimacy, compression, stack density, and whether the breath serves the phrase decide.

position_a: Use automatic breath detection across the whole vocal
position_b: Edit breaths manually one by one
what_decides: Long consistent sessions favor detection; important exposed vocals and ambiguous consonants favor manual review.

position_a: A zero crossing guarantees a click-free edit
position_b: A short crossfade is still required
what_decides: Complex/stereo waveforms, DC offset, and level differences mean zero crossing is only one diagnostic aid.

position_a: Use the shortest possible crossfade
position_b: Use a longer crossfade to blend tone and ambience
what_decides: Transient material favors short fades; sustained or room-different material may require longer fades or a different take.

position_a: Use equal-gain crossfades
position_b: Use equal-power crossfades
what_decides: Correlation, level, overlap, and the perceived dip or swell decide; audition both at fixed boundaries.

position_a: Finish the comp before tuning and cleanup
position_b: Tune or clean each take before comping
what_decides: Comp-first minimizes wasted work; pre-processing may help audition difficult takes but risks bias and duplication.

position_a: Choose the technically cleanest take
position_b: Choose the emotionally strongest take and repair it
what_decides: The severity of defects, repair artifacts, and musical role decide; compare in context.

position_a: Quantize the whole performance
position_b: Edit only obvious timing conflicts manually
what_decides: Stable grid-based genres favor bounded quantization; rubato, acoustic phrasing, and mixed intentional timing favor manual edits.

position_a: Make the performance follow the project grid
position_b: Make the tempo map follow the performance
what_decides: Loop-driven arrangements favor the grid; expressive foundational performances may define tempo.

position_a: Align doubles tightly
position_b: Preserve loose timing for width and humanity
what_decides: Lyric intelligibility and rhythmic precision favor tighter onsets; ensemble width and energy favor controlled variation.

position_a: Align complete vocal phrases
position_b: Align consonants but leave vowels less constrained
what_decides: Unison pop precision may favor more alignment; natural stacks and harmonies often benefit from protected sustains.

position_a: Use automatic alignment tools
position_b: Manually edit each phrase
what_decides: Large consistent stacks favor automation with protected areas; complex phrasing and exposed leads require manual review.

position_a: Repair timing with Flex Time
position_b: Choose another take instead
what_decides: Small local timing defects favor Flex; extreme stretch, artifact-prone material, or stronger alternate performances favor comping.

position_a: Use polyphonic stretching for guitar/piano
position_b: Use slicing for transient-rich parts
what_decides: Sustained harmonic continuity favors polyphonic methods; isolated attacks with acceptable gaps may favor slicing.

position_a: Remove bleed from every close microphone
position_b: Keep bleed as part of the instrument and room
what_decides: Phase coherence, genre, room quality, and exposure determine whether bleed supports or distracts.

position_a: Time-align room microphones to close mics
position_b: Preserve natural room arrival time
what_decides: Cancellation problems may justify movement; depth and spatial impression often depend on delay.

position_a: Remove all audible hiss
position_b: Use conservative reduction and accept residual noise
what_decides: Exposed speech-like material may tolerate more repair; music, tails, breath, and harmonics often reveal artifacts.

position_a: Repair every defect in post
position_b: Re-record the passage
what_decides: Unique performance or unavailable session favors repair; severe artifacts and easy access favor re-recording.

position_a: Consolidate after every edit phase
position_b: Keep live edits until final approval
what_decides: CPU/collaboration may favor interim prints, but revision risk favors late consolidation with archived sources.

position_a: Add layers until the sound is big enough
position_b: Replace or redesign the primary source
what_decides: A missing specific role may justify a support; broad weakness usually calls for a stronger primary.

position_a: Keep every layer full and natural
position_b: Filter each layer to its assigned role
what_decides: Full-range character matters for identity; role filtering is useful only where real overlap exists.

position_a: Every layer should sound good solo
position_b: Support layers may sound incomplete alone
what_decides: Standalone reuse favors full tone; a fused composite often needs role-limited supports.

position_a: Limit every composite to two layers
position_b: Use as many layers as the sound requires
what_decides: Clarity and efficiency favor few layers; complex cinematic or ensemble designs may justify more when every role is distinct.

position_a: Sample-align every layer exactly
position_b: Align by ear and accept controlled offset
what_decides: Related low-frequency samples often need careful timing; ensemble/room layers may benefit from natural spread.

position_a: Flip polarity before moving samples
position_b: Nudge timing before trying polarity
what_decides: Polarity is a fast binary test; actual arrival-time differences may require timing, but both should be isolated.

position_a: Tune all drum layers to the song
position_b: Leave transient drum layers untuned
what_decides: Sustained/ringing components make tuning relevant; short noise-like transients may not need exact pitch.

position_a: Use real double performances
position_b: Duplicate and microshift one performance
what_decides: Real doubles add organic variance; microshift is faster and controlled but carries phase/mono risks.

position_a: Keep an essential mono/center core
position_b: Make every layer wide for maximum size
what_decides: Translation and focal stability favor a core; decorative atmospheres can be intentionally fragile.

position_a: Keep all sub information mono
position_b: Preserve natural stereo low-frequency information
what_decides: Club/mono translation favors stable sub; real room or stereo instruments may retain some low width if cancellation is controlled.

position_a: Use EQ to create frequency slots
position_b: Change register, voicing, rhythm, and source choice first
what_decides: Static overlapping sources may need EQ, but musical allocation often solves masking more naturally.

position_a: Process all layers on one bus for glue
position_b: Process each layer separately before summing
what_decides: Shared processing fuses behavior; source-specific conflicts and triggers need individual control.

position_a: Use Folder Stacks for all layer groups
position_b: Use Summing Stacks for layered instruments
what_decides: Organization-only needs favor Folder; shared routing/processing and one composite fader favor Summing.

position_a: Resample layered instruments early
position_b: Keep layers editable throughout production
what_decides: Creative commitment and CPU favor printing; later arrangement, tuning, and balance revision favor live layers.

position_a: Keep the layered instrument consistent through the song
position_b: Change layers by section
what_decides: Continuity favors static identity; contrast and masking control favor section-specific layers.

position_a: Add a separate attack layer
position_b: Shape the original transient
what_decides: A missing unique attack timbre favors layering; simple envelope imbalance favors transient shaping.

position_a: Add a dedicated sub layer
position_b: Generate harmonics or redesign one bass source
what_decides: Missing fundamental weight favors sub; translation problems often need upper harmonics rather than more sub.

position_a: Add an ambience recording
position_b: Use reverb/delay to create atmosphere
what_decides: Specific location and texture favor recorded ambience; coherent controllable space favors effects.

position_a: Align backing vocals into one pad
position_b: Preserve independent ensemble timing
what_decides: Modern precise stacks favor tighter onsets; choir-like width and humanity favor controlled differences.

position_a: Keep breaths in every vocal layer
position_b: Keep one lead breath and reduce support breaths
what_decides: Natural ensemble realism may retain several; clarity and noise control often favor one anchor.

position_a: Double the exact guitar part
position_b: Use complementary voicings or rhythms
what_decides: Wall-of-guitars aesthetics favor doubles; clarity and harmonic detail favor complementary arrangement.

position_a: Layer piano and synth with the same full voicing
position_b: Assign piano transient and synth sustain/register roles
what_decides: Dense impact may justify doubling; most mixes benefit from complementary envelope and voicing.

position_a: Judge each layer by muting in context
position_b: Solo each layer to inspect its quality
what_decides: Context determines role; solo is still useful for artifacts and source defects but not final contribution.

position_a: Turn texture up until clearly audible
position_b: Keep texture below separate-event perception
what_decides: Featured sound design may be obvious; support texture often works best when its absence is noticed.
